TITLE: Baseline for Corruption Robustness in Generative Modeling
PROPOSAL: We compare the performance of state-of-the-art diffusion models and flow-based models under a variety of corruption scenarios, including different noise types, signal-to-noise ratios, and corruption patterns. We assess their ability to synthesize clean data using the corrupted observations and evaluate metrics such as PSNR and SSIM.
CONTROLS: We compare against standard implementations of AR-X and VAE models, which are not designed for corruption robustness. We also examine the effect of data augmentation using the corrupted observations.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect state-of-the-art diffusion models and flow-based models to show superior performance in generating clean data from corrupted observations, but may fail for extreme corruption scenarios. The performance of standard VAE models may not degrade as much as diffusion models due to their simpler learning objectives.

The goal of this proposal is to set a baseline for the challenges that follow, and understand how_existing models perform under realistic corruption scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learning Inverse Generative Models with Controllable Outputs
PROPOSAL: We propose to use a hybrid approach that combines adversarial training with VAEs to learn an inverse generative model that takes corrupted inputs and outputs clean samples with controllable properties. Specifically, we use a discriminator to regularize the generator, and a separate encoder to map corrupted inputs to their corresponding clean samples. We train this model using a combination of adversarial loss and evidence lower bound (ELBO) regularization.
CONTROLS: We ablate the two key components, discriminator and encoder, to understand their individual contributions to model performance. We also compare our approach to Empirical Bayes with diffusion models, as well as AR-X and VAE models.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our proposed model should significantly outperform baselines in generating clean outputs from corrupted inputs, especially when controlling for specific properties such as noise level or signal-to-noise ratio. However, it may struggle with learning complex inverse mappings without sufficient training data.

This proposal assesses the feasibility of learning an inverse generative model that can learn complex mappings between corrupted inputs and clean samples.

We combine adversarial training with the evidence lower bound (ELBO), minimizing the difference Φ(x) - x while penalizing Φ(y) ≠ x to disentangle the mapping function w.r.t the true signal x and the noisy measurements y. We train this revised model using a combination of adversarial loss and ELBO regularization.
CONTROLS: The same ablations and comparisons as before (two key components, discriminator and encoder).
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our revised model should significantly improve over the initial one, due to more targeted and effective training objectives. However, potential convergence issues with a too challenging learning objective should still be considered.

The target remains learning an inverse mapping that disentangles the noisy observations y from true signal x, and the improvement aims at faster and stable converging to a better mapping.

TITLE: Real-World Evaluation across Experimental Domains
PROPOSAL: We extend the baseline experiment and evaluate corruption robustness in real-world data across different experimental domains, including image inpainting, image deblurring, JPEG compression artifact removal, and quasar spectra reconstruction. This will provide a comprehensive understanding of the model's performance in diverse applications.

TITLE: Adversarial-regularized Invertible Neural Networks
PROPOSAL: We introduce an invertible neural network (INN) that incorporates an additional adversarial regularization term to encourage the network to learn an invertible mapping between the input and output. We train the INN to map corrupted inputs to clean samples, and evaluate its performance in recovering the true signal from noisy observations.
CONTROLS: We compare our INN model to the regularized adversarial training approach in proposal 2, and also evaluate its performance in real-world domains (evaluation task 3).
COST: 600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The INN model should excel in recovering the true signal from noisy observations, thanks to its invertible nature and adversarial regularization. However, it may face challenges in handling complex corruption scenarios or non-linear mapping functions.

This new proposal introduces an alternative method for improving corruption robustness, focusing on learning an invertible neural network to better match the data encoding.

TITLE: Theoretical Guarantees for Corruption Robustness
PROPOSAL: We provide a theoretical framework for understanding the corruption robustness of deep generative models. Specifically, we prove that under certain conditions, our adversarial-regularized invertible neural networks (ARINNs) are guaranteed to converge to the true distribution, even in the presence of noisy and corrupted observations. We also derive a bound on the error of the inverted samples and show that it decreases exponentially with the number of iterations.
CONTROLS: We compare our theoretical results to existing bounds and guarantees in the literature.
COST: N/A
PREDICTION: Our theoretical framework should provide a rigorous foundation for understanding and analyzing the corruption robustness of deep generative models. However, the choice of conditions and the derivation of the bounds may be challenging and require further investigation.

This proposal provides a theoretical foundation to the set of experiments, reinforcing the overall framework of scalable generative models for inverse problems.

Specifically, use a neural network F_theta to approximate the simulator F, with learnable parameters theta, and a neural operator U_phi to learn the integral operator K, with learnable parameters phi. Define a loss function that enforces the reproduction of the observed data mu in terms of the learned priors K U_phi \* pi, where pi is parameterized by a neural density estimator. Train the model by alternately optimizing the parameters theta and phi, with the goal of minimizing the loss.

TITLE: Unsupervised Neural Operator Learning for Inverse Problems
PROPOSAL: 
Develop an unsupervised neural operator learning framework for modeling the inverse problem FA(x) = y, where F: X -> Y is the corrupted forward map and A(x) represents the clean data. Specifically, define a neural operator U_phi that learns to map the measurements y back to the clean data space, and an encoder E_theta that maps the clean data space to a latent space. Define a reconstruction loss that encourages the neural operator U_phi to reconstruct the clean data given the measurements, and an autoencoding loss that encourages the encoder E_theta to preserve the structure of the clean data in the latent space. Train the model jointly, with the goal of minimizing the reconstruction loss and preserving the structure of the clean data in the latent space.
CONTROLS: 
 Best-case: Using a large dataset of paired clean and corrupted measurements with well-conditioned forward operators, we expect to demonstrate state-of-the-art reconstruction performance and latent space preservation.
 Cost: 50 GPU-hours (possibly as few as 1 hour if simulated forward operators are assumed) with masked embeddings.
PREDICTION: If successful, we expect the method to identify a valid neural operator U_phi that can reconstruct the clean data from the measurements, with potential applications in inverse problems. Failure could arise from difficulties in choosing the neural architecture and training procedure or complexities in the forward map F.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Transfer Learning for Neural Operator-based Inverse Problems
PROPOSAL: 
Investigate the possibility of transferring knowledge from pre-trained neural operators to tackle new inverse problems with different forward maps or corrupted observations. Specifically, design a transfer learning framework that leverages the learned representations from a pre-trained neural operator for a related inverse problem, and adapt these representations to the new inverse problem using a fine-tuning procedure. Evaluate the effectiveness of transfer learning for different types of pre-training, including pre-training on synthetic data, pre-training on real-world data, and pre-training on a combination of both.
CONTROLS: 
 Best-case: We expect to demonstrate significant performance gains and reduced training times when using transfer learning for related inverse problems.
 Cost: 80 GPU-hours, depending on the size of the pre-trained models and the complexity of the new inverse problem.
PREDICTION: If successful, we expect the transfer learning approach to enable efficient and accurate solution of new inverse problems, by leveraging the knowledge learned from related problems. Failure could arise from difficulties in aligning the pre-trained and new tasks, or improperly parameterizing the fine-tuning procedure.

ACTION: REVISE 5
TITLE: Transfer Learning for Neural Operator-based Inverse Problems with Adversarial Training
PROPOSAL: 
Modify the transfer learning framework to incorporate adversarial training, which aims to enhance the robustness and domain adaptation capabilities of the pre-trained neural operator. Specifically, design an adversarial training procedure that forces the pre-trained neural operator to be unaffected by adversarial corruptions in the data or the corrupted forward map. This can be achieved by introducing an additional discriminator network that tries to distinguish between real and adversarial samples. The goal is to improve the robustness of transfer learning for neural operator-based inverse problems and enable the model to generalize better across different inverse problems.
CONTROLS: 
 Best-case: We expect to demonstrate improved robustness and domain adaptation performance when using adversarial training for transfer learning.
 Cost: 120 GPU-hours, depending on the complexity of the adversarial training procedure and the number of adversarial samples generated.
PREDICTION: If successful, we expect the adversarial training approach to significantly improve the robustness and domain adaptation capabilities of transfer learning for neural operator-based inverse problems. Failure could arise from difficulties in balancing the learning rates of the generator and discriminator, or overfitting to the adversarial samples.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Scalable Neural Operator Networks for Large-Scale Inverse Problems
PROPOSAL: 
Develop a scalable neural operator network architecture that can handle large-scale inverse problems with millions of data points and high-dimensional feature spaces. Specifically, propose a distributed neural operator architecture that uses a hierarchical structure of small nodes, each with a local neural operator, to learn the mapping between the input and output of the forward map. The local neural operators are then combined using a global aggregation operator to produce the learned mapping. Evaluate the scalability and performance of the proposed architecture on large-scale inverse problems in various fields, including image analysis, signal processing, and scientific computing.
CONTROLS: 
 Best-case: We expect to demonstrate a significant reduction in computational resources and time required to solve large-scale inverse problems, while maintaining or improving the accuracy of the solutions.
 Cost: 400 GPU-hours, depending on the size of the large-scale inverse problem and the complexity of the hierarchical neural operator architecture.
PREDICTION: If successful, we expect the scalable neural operator network to enable the efficient solution of large-scale inverse problems in various fields, with implications for fields such as materials science, climate modeling, and medical imaging. Failure could arise from difficulties in designing a suitable hierarchical neural operator architecture, or limitations in the computational resources available.

PROPOSAL: Explore the use of normalizing flows as a potential framework for inverse generative modeling under a black-box forward simulator F. We will explore the idea of learning an invertible mapping g such that the push-forward measure of pi under g matches the empirical distribution of corrupted observations mu. A neural network can be trained to learn g such that the divergence between the push-forward measure and mu is minimized.
CONTROLS: Train normalizing flows on datasets where the clean observations are available, such as CelebA-HQ and LSUN.
